city.name: Stillwater
city.description: A post-industrial river city of about 40,000. Its kilns and dye works closed decades ago; its economy now turns on a single automated logistics centre, a council tower and a long tail of care, retail and gig work. Public services are coordinated from the Council Tower, whose predictive systems schedule buses, allocate housing and set patrol routes. The river runs slow and brown through Lowbank. Officially, nothing much happens in Stillwater.

Regulatory Appeal Filed.explain: They formally appeal the refusal to release information, but polite non-answers slowly drain their urgency.

Relocation Deferred.explain: They look for work elsewhere, but a heavy workload and refused leave make leaving the city hard.

Retained in Post.explain: They remain head librarian, their questions steered into local history work, kept in place by close friendships.

Persistent Data Opacity.explain: They use cash, paper notes and a switched-off phone, making their life much harder to track or predict.

Natural Death.explain: They die late in life of an unknown cause, since their medical records are too thin to say.

Delayed Chest Imaging.explain: They have the chest X-ray eventually, but late, after refusing to be escorted by a support worker.

Supervised Treatment Initiation.explain: They begin treatment for a suspected lung infection, with medicine handed out under supervision at the shelter where a bed is held.

Associate Screening Flag.explain: The people who share shelters and nights outdoors with them are flagged to be tested for infection too.

Loss to Follow-Up.explain: They stop the treatment partway and lose touch with doctors, partly because they have no address to be contacted at.

Failed Re-entry Attempt.plain: Fails to get back into work
Failed Re-entry Attempt.explain: They try to find a job or open a bank account without an address, but it fails; old warehouse jobs are gone.

Death, Respiratory Failure.explain: They die by the river from a long-untreated lung illness, made worse by cold and not enough food.

Untreated pulmonary infection.explain: They are expected to die in 2055, aged 49, from a lung infection that never got treated.

Antihypertensive Adherence Established.explain: They collect blood pressure medicine and get checked at the library, keeping it partly under control as long as they keep visiting daily.

Winter Bed Secured.plain: Gets a reliable winter shelter bed
Winter Bed Secured.explain: They get a standing shelter bed for winter, so they sleep outside less, though still on some nights.

Respiratory Exposure Screen.explain: They are tested after spending months near someone with a suspected lung infection, and may still carry a hidden infection.

Social Network Contraction.explain: Their friends move away, are kept apart, or withdraw, leaving only library staff and a distant sibling to talk to.

Hypertensive Crisis Admission.explain: When medicine or a bed slips, their blood pressure spikes dangerously; they spend a short time in hospital, then return to the shelter.

Terminal Cerebrovascular Event.explain: Worn down by years of near-street living and poor food, they have a fatal stroke at a shelter or library.

Stroke.explain: They are expected to die of a stroke in 2060, aged 75.

Repair Ticket Closed.explain: The mould in their flat is cleaned up quickly and the complaint is closed, ending outside questions about it.

Referral Quietly Closed.explain: An automatic report to child services is closed without action; they never learn it existed, and their worry about losing their child eases.

Child Respiratory Improvement.explain: Their child wheezes less once the damp is gone, needs fewer clinic visits, and goes to school more regularly.

Managed Low-Income Plateau.explain: They keep an insecure care job with unpaid travel, stay on antidepressants long-term, and their low mood is managed, not cured.

Care Role Progression.explain: They look for steadier hours or a senior care role as their child starts secondary school, but success is unclear.

Occupational Injury / Exit.explain: Years of lifting people in care work leave them with lasting physical pain, so they stop working early and go on disability benefits.

Forecourt Assembly Proceeds.explain: They ignore official warnings and return to the council building with a friend to keep pushing for the tenants' group.

Enforcement Agent Referral.explain: With no income to take fines from, their unpaid fines and council tax go to bailiffs and grow with extra charges.

Tenancy Arrears Proceedings.explain: If they withhold charges, the council takes them to court over arrears on their home, and they attend and fight it.

Campaign Attrition.explain: Members leave after rumours about their past debts spread, leaving only a few, so they go back to campaigning alone.

Unobserved Economic Activity.explain: They stay out of official work and benefits, possibly getting by on cash delivery or driving jobs.

Cardiometabolic Event.explain: They may suffer a heart-related health crisis or growing difficulty walking, while living on a fifth floor with an often-broken lift.

Pool Retention.explain: They keep getting agency shifts at the warehouse, earning some declared wages instead of only cash, for now.

Informal Network Lapse.explain: A check on their cash deposits ends without penalty, and their informal friends and contacts drift away.

Agency Pool Release.explain: Machines take over the warehouse, their shifts dwindle below what they need to live on, as happened before.

Informal Economy Return.explain: They go back to earning cash informally, sometimes stay out overnight, fall behind on phone bills and pawn belongings.

Relocation / Kerrow.explain: They leave the city for warehouse jobs in a nearby town and drop out of the system's view.

Kept On Through Winter.explain: They keep low-paid cash work at the scrapyard all winter, giving their day a routine that fits their medicine pickups.

Volunteer Placement Cleared.explain: A background check flag is cleared, so they can start supervised volunteering at the library if they don't pull out.

Supervised Family Contact.explain: They meet their child and grandchild for a second Christmas, as long as their drug tests stay clean.

Continued Police Contact.explain: Police keep searching them because of their record, finding nothing, which adds stress and risk of relapse.

Stable Maintenance Equilibrium.explain: They see their grandchild regularly and stay on long-term methadone rather than quitting entirely.

Exit From Labour.explain: As their body weakens in their sixties, casual work ends and they live on benefits in their flat.

Death, Natural Causes.explain: They die around age 72 from heart and lung strain after decades of opioid use.

Cardiorespiratory failure.plain: Dies of heart and lung failure
Cardiorespiratory failure.explain: They are expected to die in 2066, aged 72, when the heart and lungs give out.

Supervised Collection Resumed.explain: They pick up antidepressants only at the clinic each Tuesday with a neighbour, at the late spouse's old appointment time.

Secondary Collector Departs.explain: A young helper who also collected their medicine moves away to university, leaving just one person helping.

Will Revision.explain: They update their will themselves without a lawyer, a common step when preparing for death.

Undetected Domestic Fall.explain: They may fall or collapse at home and lie there over a day before anyone finds them.

Collector Link Degrades.explain: The neighbour who goes with them to collect medicine starts missing visits due to home troubles.

Silent Treatment Withdrawal.explain: They may quietly stop their medication and stop going to the clinic, despite reminder calls.

Frailty / Cardiac Decline.explain: Living alone in old age after losing a spouse, their heart weakens and they keep losing weight; home care is offered.

Heart failure / Frailty.explain: They are expected to die in 2057, aged 88, from heart failure and frailty.

External Disclosure Attempt.explain: They may try taking concerns about the council's housing algorithm to outside appeals or journalists, though less likely after being refused.

Separation / Relocation.explain: Their engagement is called off; new evening and weekend shifts cut time together and contact with supportive colleagues.

Formal Complaint Lodged.explain: They file an official complaint after a public meeting fails to answer their questions, delayed by polite, empty replies.

Out-of-City Move.explain: They may leave for a library job elsewhere, though fixed work commitments and refused leave make interviews hard.

Contained Continuity.explain: If they stay, they lead a local memory project, keep private notes offline, and stop asking questions publicly.

Hypertension Diagnosis.explain: They may be diagnosed with long-term high blood pressure from stress, working evenings and weekends and living alone.

Blood Pressure Partially Controlled.explain: They collect regular blood pressure pills, and readings improve somewhat, as long as they keep a usable mailing address.

Routine Consolidated.explain: Their informal help at the library becomes an official volunteer role, and their days shrink to a fixed library routine.

Respiratory Contact Follow-up.explain: The person is screened after contact with someone with a long cough, and may need follow-up treatment for a hidden infection.

Housing Queue Static.explain: The person stays homeless, with a low-priority housing application that does not move up the long waiting list.

Anchor Disruption.explain: A supportive librarian may leave, the person loses informal protection at the library, and goes back to sleeping under an underpass.

Cerebrovascular Warning Event.explain: After missing blood pressure pills while without a stable address, the person suffers a warning stroke and is admitted to hospital.

Death / Stroke.explain: The person dies of a stroke after years of high blood pressure and homelessness, likely near the shelter or library.

Referral Closed / NFA.explain: A child-protection referral is closed without a visit, easing the person's fear of losing custody, though complaints remain on file.

Debt Consolidation Plan.explain: The person repays debts through small weekly deductions, clearing them by late 2055 if work hours hold up.

Organising Contact Lapses.explain: Once their immediate problems are fixed, the person drifts away from the tenants' group and stops pursuing complaints.

Chronic Managed Depression.explain: The person stays on antidepressants long-term, with persistent low mood and poor sleep from work and solo parenting.

Zero-Hours Plateau.explain: The person keeps doing home care on unpredictable hours, never gets a secure contract, and relies on benefits to get by.

Son Leaves Home.explain: The person's son becomes an adult and leaves home, leaving them living alone in council housing, still doing care work.

Early Work Exit.plain: Leaves work due to ill health
Early Work Exit.explain: Years of physical strain, stress and low pay cause high blood pressure and injuries, forcing the person onto sickness benefits.

Supervised Pool Placement.explain: They start official agency work but, due to a background check note, may only work on one supervised crew.

Income Review Outcome.explain: Investigators decide some cash deposits were unreported earnings, leading to a small repayment plan or a formal warning.

Network Re-engagement.explain: After losing official income, they go back to old contacts and off-the-books cash work that authorities cannot track.

Housing Loss.explain: The person loses their rented room and ends up sleeping rough on and off.

Tenant Protest Participation.explain: The person joins a tenants' protest outside the council building with a neighbour.

Clinical Anchor Held.explain: The person keeps taking methadone daily at a set clinic time, with clean drug tests and dose reduction put on hold.

Repeat Stop and Search.explain: Police stop and search the person again, finding nothing, as protest involvement makes them more noticeable while on a suspended sentence.

Family Contact Renewed.explain: The person meets their daughter and grandson again at Christmas, allowed only while drug tests stay clean.

Volunteer Path Closed.explain: Their library volunteering application is never answered, so they spend spare time on tenant organising instead.

Loss of Casual Work.explain: The person's seasonal cash work ends, leaving no income and nothing structuring the day except the clinic visit.

Relapse.explain: Without work or routine, the person starts using opioids again, at high overdose risk from lowered tolerance, and loses family contact.

Unsanctioned Collection Link.explain: They rely on a chosen neighbour, not the official volunteer, to pick up their antidepressants occasionally.

Secondary Link Departure.explain: A neighbour's daughter who helped collect medicine moves away to university, leaving them with one fewer local connection.

Unassisted Will Revision.explain: The person updates their will themselves, delayed but not stopped by a long wait for legal help.

Neighbour Link Erosion.explain: Their only remaining helper neighbour faces job and marriage troubles, becoming less available, with nobody to replace that support.

Fall / Acute Admission.explain: The person falls or suddenly worsens at home and is hospitalised, weakened by weight loss, untreated blood pressure and poor mobility.

Residential Care Placement.explain: With no family nearby, the person goes from hospital into a care home and their house is put up for sale.

Cardiac failure, self-neglect.explain: The person dies at 87 in 2056 from heart failure, worsened by being unable to look after themselves.

Library Routine Formalised.explain: The person's unpaid shelving work at the library becomes a named volunteer role, with a set chair and a weekly visiting companion.

Family Contact Contained.plain: Keeps in touch with family online
Family Contact Contained.explain: They keep contacting family only by library email, refusing money offered, and are not expected to leave the city.

Hypertensive Crisis.plain: Rushed to clinic with dangerous blood pressure
Hypertensive Crisis.explain: The person suffers a blood pressure emergency needing urgent clinic care, made less likely by repeat prescriptions and monthly checks at the library.

Respiratory Infection.plain: Catches chest infection from sick man
Respiratory Infection.explain: They catch a lung infection from a seriously ill man sharing the library, a risk reduced by separating their computer times.

Supported Placement Transfer.explain: The person is moved into long-term supported housing for over-65s instead of getting a council flat; the housing application lapses unresolved.

Referral Closed, NFA.explain: A concern sent to children's services is closed without a home visit; the family stays together and the person never learns of it.

Caseworker Dependency Established.explain: Benefit penalties stop and appointments fit school hours, but everything goes through one caseworker and the person stops trying to appeal decisions.

Static Low-Wage Tenure.plain: Stuck in poorly paid care job
Static Low-Wage Tenure.explain: They stay on insecure, low-paid care work without paid travel, getting slightly steadier hours but remaining on a low income.

Occupational Injury / Workforce Exit.explain: Years of lifting in home care cause lasting injury, so the person works less and moves onto sickness benefits managed by a caseworker.

Zone D Role Accepted.plain: Takes sideways job with pay rise
Zone D Role Accepted.explain: The person accepts a same-level supervisory job with a retention bonus, while that area is being automated over the next years.

Retention Stabilised.explain: They stay at the company thanks to a confirmed pay rise and health support, performing steadily but never promoted, with workplace rivalry quiet.

Alcohol-Related Health Episode.explain: Heavy drinking, untreated high blood pressure and insomnia cause a health crisis and time off sick, less likely if they attend the clinic.

Role Consolidation / Exit.explain: The person's scheduling job is taken over by a computer forecasting system, and they leave with an improved redundancy payout.

Solitary Middle Age.explain: They live alone in a smaller home with less income, see mostly their daughter, and only sometimes manage heart health.

Delayed Departure.explain: At the station the person phones their father rather than leaving, delaying departure by a few days amid family troubles.

University Enrolment.explain: They enrol on a social work degree at university, with a $600 transfer from their father covering initial costs.

Housing Allocation Inquiry.explain: Through coursework the person formally looks into how the city's housing waiting list decides who gets homes, using a known case.

Social Work Qualification.explain: They qualify in social work and look for a first job; jobs near university are encouraged, home-city applications slowed down.

Casework Application Deferred.explain: The person applies for social work in a poor area back home, but it is held up, so they keep their current job.

Permanent Relocation.explain: They settle permanently elsewhere, returning only to visit their father, and gradually disappear from the city's records.

Reserved Bed Declined.explain: They refuse the reserved shelter bed and curfew, staying instead between a church, the library and time with a friend.

Respiratory Exposure Finding.explain: They spend days near a sick, untested friend and will likely test positive for a lung infection if screened.

Antihypertensive Lapse.explain: They only sometimes pick up blood pressure medication, so their blood pressure stays too high.

Path Exit / Rehousing.explain: They unexpectedly get off the streets, either moving in with a sister or getting a council flat years later.

Housing Escalation (Suppressed).explain: They try to complain about their housing with outside help, but official routing and a closure letter shut it down.

Withdrawal From Organising.explain: They drop out of the tenants' meetings after the time moves to clash with their care work shifts.

Sustained Precarious Employment.explain: They keep working zero-hours care shifts on low pay, with a steadier contract possible but not promised.

Managed Chronic Low Mood.explain: Their benefits settle down and they stay on long-term antidepressants, but the depression could return at any time.

Exit From Care Work.plain: Body forces end of care work
Exit From Care Work.explain: Years of physical strain end their care job in their early fifties, leaving them on disability benefits in the same flat.

Board Escalation Against Shore.explain: They use direct access to company bosses to renew accusations against a colleague's flawed forecasting system.

Daughter Leaves Household.explain: Their daughter moves away to university, and they mostly hear about her through their ex-partner.

Zone D Delivery / Retention.explain: They hit project deadlines while 44 jobs are cut, and receive extra pay to stay at the company.

Hypertension / Hazardous Drinking.explain: Their drinking grows to a medically harmful level, alongside high blood pressure and insomnia treated with sleeping pills.

Career Plateau / Isolation.explain: They settle for a lesser regional job, live alone and see their daughter only occasionally.

Daughter Leaves Home.explain: Their daughter, their closest bond, moves away to university, leaving the couple alone and growing apart.

Individual Counselling Uptake.explain: They begin solo counselling on Thursday evenings, replacing some time spent in the park and a skipped couples session.

Housing Advocacy Escalation.explain: They escalate the flat's mould problem beyond the housing office, to child protection or a local councillor.

New Partnership.explain: After separating, they openly partner with a work colleague and settle into a stable home life locally.

Hours Restored.explain: Their reduced work hours end and they return to nearly full-time teaching at the same primary school.
